text: Container Insights isn't a separate monitoring product — it's CloudWatch's own ContainerInsights namespace, populated by agents you deploy into the cluster, with dashboards organized around clusters, nodes, pods, and containers instead of raw EC2 instances. This lesson covers how those metrics actually get collected on EKS, how logs travel through a completely separate pipeline, and where to look first on a real pod-level incident.

The CloudWatch agent publishes metrics at four levels. Cluster gives you aggregate node and pod counts across the whole thing. Node gives you per-node CPU, memory, and network usage — where you'd catch a node running hot before pods on it start getting evicted. Pod gives you usage against that pod's own requests and limits. Container drills in further, useful the moment a pod runs more than one container and you need to know which one is actually consuming the resources.

pod_memory_utilization_over_pod_limit is the metric that explains an OOMKilled pod after the fact — it measures usage against the pod's own configured limit, not some cluster-wide average. An alarm on this metric crossing 90%, scoped to a specific cluster, namespace, and pod name, is a real leading indicator you'd set up before the kill happens, not just a postmortem artifact you check afterward.

The CloudWatch agent is deployed as a DaemonSet, meaning Kubernetes schedules exactly one agent pod onto every node automatically, including new nodes added by autoscaling — no manual step. Fluent Bit runs as its own separate DaemonSet, tailing container stdout and stderr on every node and shipping it into CloudWatch Logs log groups like slash aws slash containerinsights slash your-cluster slash application. That's a deliberate split: metrics and logs are different kinds of telemetry, moving through two different pipelines, exactly like Chapter 1 and Lesson 9 already established.

Once those logs land in CloudWatch Logs, they're queryable with the exact same fields, filter, stats, and parse syntax from Lesson 9 — nothing new to learn just because the source is a container instead of an EC2 instance. Walk a real incident: a composite alarm on pod memory pressure pages on-call, the Container Insights dashboard shows which specific pod is climbing, and a Logs Insights query scoped to that pod and time window surfaces what the application was actually doing right before it ran out of headroom.

That closes this chapter: CloudWatch metrics and Logs Insights queries, alarms and composite alarms that don't flap, X-Ray for distributed tracing, and now Container Insights applying all of it to EKS workloads specifically — cluster, node, pod, and container metrics from the CloudWatch agent, logs from Fluent Bit, and the same query language tying both together on a real incident.
